Maladaptive Strategies.value: control eating strictly to feel in control
I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
go along with whatever others want to feel safe

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel isolated and set apart from others
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette: Kabir, a forty-one-year-old South Asian man, finds that his daily patrols through the state park constantly place him in the exact environment that fuels his distress. Three years earlier, a border incident had dragged him into a dim holding cell where armed captors in heavy uniforms controlled every movement, forcing him to sit in silence while others were paraded past for their own survival. Now, when a fellow hiker loudly recounts army deployment stories along the park’s paved trail, the sharp cadence of those military topics directly fuels his conviction that he is permanently humiliated by what he endured. Those auditory triggers consistently revive the fragmented, picture-like recollections of his confinement, each frozen moment locking into place with a sudden, sharp pain in his ribs and forearms where the restraints had bitten him. His PCL-5 score of forty confirmed the moderate but relentless burden of his symptoms, yet the clinical labels mean little compared to the lived reality that the constant exposure to those triggers also reinforces his negative view of himself, making him believe he was uniquely broken compared to others who would never have ended up captured. Because he carries this belief of personal failure into his daily routine, even a passerby’s glance on the ranger station porch makes him acutely aware of himself, which in turn keeps the original triggers of his captivity perpetually active. Over the following months, the fragmented recollections refused to fade into the background. Each time the disjointed frames of his captivity returned with such visceral clarity, they reinforced his belief that he was uniquely humiliated and isolated. His conviction that he was set apart from ordinary life directly pulled the same picture-like memories back to the surface every time he felt disconnected from his partner. The way these recollections surfaced constantly pushed his body toward a state of low-grade alarm. Whenever a tourist’s sudden step across a gravel path made him flinch, the physical jolt of being startled would immediately pull him back into those same snapshot memories, confirming that the danger was never truly over. The physiological terror of those startle responses also reinforced his conviction that he could never truly trust that he was safe, even when his supervisor assured him the trails were secure. As his distrust of safety deepened, it further hardened his negative view of himself, making him feel completely isolated and setting him apart from anyone who hadn’t survived what he had. Working as a park ranger eventually placed Kabir directly in the path of his triggers, but he had developed a rigid set of coping habits to manage the rising tide of fear. The sudden return of those physical pains and fragmented images directly pushes him toward revenge fantasies and strict dietary control to regain a sense of dominance. This people-pleasing compulsion, adopted to keep others from turning hostile, meant he would agree to extra shifts or silent upsets just to avoid conflict. However, these survival habits quickly backfired; the emotional numbness he cultivated through restrictive eating and silent compliance only left him more vulnerable to sudden emotional flashbacks, while the isolation his people-pleasing bred further convinced him that he was uniquely broken. The constant restriction of his food intake also leaves his nervous system permanently on edge, making him react as if he is in danger whenever unexpected movement occurs nearby. The silence he kept to avoid scrutiny also meant he could no longer process his fears, which only intensified his startle response and left him even more hypersensitive to anyone in uniform or discussing military affairs, locking him back into the cycle. The breaking point came when his partner noticed him skipping meals while staring blankly at his patrol radio, unable to explain the sudden panic that seized him during a routine equipment check. Kabir finally sought help because the weight of his own silence had become heavier than the captivity he had escaped. He feared that without intervention, the rigid control and relentless shame would permanently isolate him from the life he wanted, though he secretly hoped a therapist might help him untangle the fear that still dictated his every move.
